title: dry rot fungus (Serpula lacrymans): which tools to run

text.text: The closest species with at least 100 curator-checked (Swiss-Prot) proteins is Coprinopsis cinerea; the two lineages split 171 million years ago (Mya). In human proteins searched against a species that far away (opossum, 159 Mya), the three tools with the best Fmax (the balance of finding domains and being right) were kmerseek; phmmer; MMseqs2, and kmerseek found 23% of the known Pfam domains. In the measured organism closest to this one, baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), 21% of proteins had no hit from any sequence tool, so expect a share like that to stay without a label.

# dry rot fungus (Serpula lacrymans) # UniProt reference proteome UP000008063, 14,339 proteins curl -L -o proteome.fasta.gz 'https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?query=proteome%3AUP000008063&format=fasta&compressed=true' # All reviewed Swiss-Prot proteins, the source of the labels (they include those of the nearest reviewed relative, Coprinopsis cinerea). # Swiss-Prot has about 575,000 proteins; the board measured cost against one relative's proteome of about 20,000, so expect longer runs. curl -L -o swissprot.fasta.gz 'https://ftp.uniprot.org/pub/databases/uniprot/current_release/knowledgebase/complete/uniprot_sprot.fasta.gz' # nf-core/proteinannotator 1.1.0: Pfam, FunFam and InterProScan on your proteome. # Version 1.1.0 has no option to run kmerseek; phmmer; MMseqs2; their commands follow. printf 'id,fasta\nserpula_lacrymans,proteome.fasta.gz\n' > samplesheet.csv nextflow run nf-core/proteinannotator -r 1.1.0 -profile docker --input samplesheet.csv --outdir results # -E 10.0 keeps every hit, as on the board. The board's numbers count calls above the score cut-off # that gives each tool its best Fmax; filter the output before you take labels from it. # kmerseek: its database needs build steps this page does not write out. # The command the board ran is on its tool card: tools/kmerseek.html # phmmer (quay.io/biocontainers/hmmer:3.4--hb6cb901_4 (sha256:7a2b317b8d2fd3650b4924a8482cddeb940d4a0746c6a1501ff03ac1b7439e0c)) gunzip -kf proteome.fasta.gz swissprot.fasta.gz phmmer --domtblout phmmer.domtbl --noali -E 10.0 --cpu 8 proteome.fasta swissprot.fasta > /dev/null # MMseqs2, sensitivity 7, one round (quay.io/biocontainers/mmseqs2:18.8cc5c--hd6d6fdc_0 (sha256:3503bfe576d560e550df2872af86a1ad1bcc1c06cfb7caadd3e7a95649f5f0ef)) mmseqs createdb proteome.fasta.gz q_db mmseqs createdb swissprot.fasta.gz t_db mmseqs search q_db t_db result_s7 tmp_s7 --threads 16 -s 7 --max-seqs 1000 -e 10.0 mmseqs convertalis q_db t_db result_s7 mmseqs2_s7.m8
Three tools, in the order to run them

How this was measured: 998 human proteins were searched against the proteome of opossum (Monodelphis domestica), whose lineage split from human 159 Mya. Of the 14 relatives measured that have a TimeTree age, its split age is the closest to this species' 171 Mya. Split age is a stand-in for how much proteins have changed; lineages change at different speeds. Counted: 1,399 Pfam domains in human proteins whose mean AlphaFold confidence (pLDDT, 0–100; AlphaFold DB calls 70 to 90 confident and above 90 very high) is 70-90. Tools are ranked by Fmax, the best balance of finding domains (recall) and being right (precision), 1 being perfect; the three differ by 0.019 in Fmax, a gap this one set of proteins cannot settle, so if cost matters pick the cheapest of them.

Finds 23% of Pfam domains at this distance, and 60% of the domains it reports (its calls) are right; starts a found domain a median 28 residues from where the domain starts (measured at zebrafish, 435 Mya); finds 0% of short Swiss-Prot features 2–15 residues long, such as motifs and binding sites (0% of those calls right).

Counted at the score cut-off that gives this tool its best Fmax: 0.337 on 1,399 domains; short features from 546 Swiss-Prot features. A found domain and its call overlap over a median 64% of the span they cover together.

Computer time per 1,000 proteins searched against one relative's proteome: — processor-hours (not run); cloud price — estimate (cost_usd_est). Search step only; no database-building step was recorded for it.

Human proteins searched against zebrafish (435 Mya); the grey band is the domain, every domain stretched to one width.

What no tool on this board will find for you

21.5% of 6,049 proteins of baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) had no hit from any sequence tool, even at a loose E-value below 1 (the E-value is the number of hits that size expected by chance). They were searched against Swiss-Prot with the organism's own group removed; we call these proteins dark. Of the five organisms measured, this one is closest to this species: their lineages meet at Dikarya.
no relative in Swiss-Prot (no hit at all)

The tables hold the dark share but do not split it into disordered proteins and short motifs; those two parts are not measured. Measured on: human (Homo sapiens) 15.1% of 20,600; baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) 21.5% of 6,049; nematode (Caenorhabditis elegans) 45.0% of 19,819; Lyme disease bacterium (Borrelia burgdorferi) 47.4% of 1,291; star ascidian (Botryllus schlosseri) 45.1% of 45,339.

29% estimate (expected_label_fraction_est): the share of this species' Pfam domains, not proteins, that kmerseek would be expected to find, if it finds them as often as it did in human proteins (Pfam 38.2 domains) searched against opossum (Monodelphis domestica), 159 Mya.

How: kmerseek's measured recall in each pLDDT band at that distance, weighted by the share of this species' AlphaFold models in the band. The bands with a measured recall hold 87% of its models; the rest (pLDDT 0–50, no measured domains) are left out, so for the whole proteome the share is likely lower.

Figure 2. Which domains each of the three tools finds, and which only one of them finds. The tools searched human proteins against zebrafish (435 Mya); domains whose own stretch of the protein has pLDDT 70-90. Per-domain calls were kept only for zebrafish, so this figure is at 435 Mya whatever this species' distance. A filled dot under a bar means that tool found the domain; the bar is the number of domains found by that set of tools and no other.
1,023 domains in this band; 373 of them found by none of the three. A domain counts as found when any call on it names the right Pfam family and overlaps it, at any score.

Figure 3. How Fmax falls with distance, for the three tools above. Fmax is the best balance of finding domains and being right (1 is perfect). Each mark is one relative the human proteins were searched against, all Pfam domains; where two relatives share an age (mouse and rat, 84 Mya) the line goes through their mean. Divergence times are TimeTree 5's; E. coli, with no TimeTree age, is not drawn. The step from 10 to 100 Mya takes as much room as the step from 100 to 1,000.

Tool scores and costs: results.parquet and compute.parquet, seanome/2024-kmerseek-analysis commit 7eca428b, experiment qfo_region_midi_plus. cost_usd_est is an estimate: CPU-hours times the AWS on-demand price (c7i.large $0.08925 per hour for 2 vCPU and g5.xlarge $1.006 per GPU-hour, US East, read 2026-10-15), plus GPU-hours times the GPU price. AlphaFold DB search API (models version 6) and UniProt 2026_03
https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/search?q=taxId:<taxon> AND isUniProtReferenceProteome:true AND globalMetricValue:[lo TO hi} (and UniProt proteome:<UP> AND database:alphafolddb)

answer.command:
# dry rot fungus (Serpula lacrymans)
# UniProt reference proteome UP000008063, 14,339 proteins
curl -L -o proteome.fasta.gz 'https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?query=proteome%3AUP000008063&format=fasta&compressed=true'
# All reviewed Swiss-Prot proteins, the source of the labels (they include those of the nearest reviewed relative, Coprinopsis cinerea).
# Swiss-Prot has about 575,000 proteins; the board measured cost against one relative's proteome of about 20,000, so expect longer runs.
curl -L -o swissprot.fasta.gz 'https://ftp.uniprot.org/pub/databases/uniprot/current_release/knowledgebase/complete/uniprot_sprot.fasta.gz'
# nf-core/proteinannotator 1.1.0: Pfam, FunFam and InterProScan on your proteome.
# Version 1.1.0 has no option to run kmerseek; phmmer; MMseqs2; their commands follow.
printf 'id,fasta\nserpula_lacrymans,proteome.fasta.gz\n' > samplesheet.csv
nextflow run nf-core/proteinannotator -r 1.1.0 -profile docker --input samplesheet.csv --outdir results

# -E 10.0 keeps every hit, as on the board. The board's numbers count calls above the score cut-off
# that gives each tool its best Fmax; filter the output before you take labels from it.

# kmerseek: its database needs build steps this page does not write out.
# The command the board ran is on its tool card: tools/kmerseek.html

# phmmer (quay.io/biocontainers/hmmer:3.4--hb6cb901_4 (sha256:7a2b317b8d2fd3650b4924a8482cddeb940d4a0746c6a1501ff03ac1b7439e0c))
gunzip -kf proteome.fasta.gz swissprot.fasta.gz
phmmer --domtblout phmmer.domtbl --noali -E 10.0 --cpu 8 proteome.fasta swissprot.fasta > /dev/null

# MMseqs2, sensitivity 7, one round (quay.io/biocontainers/mmseqs2:18.8cc5c--hd6d6fdc_0 (sha256:3503bfe576d560e550df2872af86a1ad1bcc1c06cfb7caadd3e7a95649f5f0ef))
mmseqs createdb proteome.fasta.gz q_db
mmseqs createdb swissprot.fasta.gz t_db
mmseqs search q_db t_db result_s7 tmp_s7 --threads 16 -s 7 --max-seqs 1000 -e 10.0
mmseqs convertalis q_db t_db result_s7 mmseqs2_s7.m8
